vignette:
Minh Tran was 40 when he came for treatment, a divorced Vietnamese American journalist who had built his career on going toward difficult stories. The event he returned to only in fragments happened while he was reporting abroad. He had been detained, interrogated, and tortured over a period he could not recount in a clear sequence. What remained with sharp force were sensory moments and the meanings he had attached to them afterward. He remembered the sound of children crying somewhere nearby, not as background noise but as something piercing and unbearable, because it existed alongside what was being done to him. He also remembered moments of dizziness and lightheadedness in his own body, when pain, fear, and hunger blurred together and he could not tell if he was about to faint. Certain names connected with that period still landed in him with immediate force; hearing them now felt less like remembering and more like being dropped without warning into the same atmosphere of danger.

In the months after he returned home, Minh found that when he tried to deliberately tell himself what had happened, the memory would not come in an ordered way. He could produce isolated pieces, but there were parts he could not access no matter how hard he tried. The missing stretches bothered him as much as the vivid pieces. At times the whole story felt unreal to him, too extreme to fit with his previous sense of his own life. He would begin to speak about it and then stop, struck by the thought that it did not sound like something that could actually have happened to him. This left him caught between fragments he could not shake and blank spaces he could not fill.

He had also come to believe that the experience showed something damaged in him. He spoke as if other people could see it on him immediately, as though the fact of what had happened had marked him in a visible way. In interviews with sources, in meetings with editors, even when ordering coffee, he often felt exposed under ordinary eye contact. He was especially troubled by the sense that he had acted against his own values during the detention. He did not elaborate easily, but he returned to the conviction that in order to survive he had behaved in ways that did not fit the person he believed himself to be. That thought carried shame as much as fear.

Back at work, his daily environment sharpened rather than softened these difficulties. As a journalist he still moved through crowded public settings, newsrooms full of sudden noises, and interviews where he had to attend closely to other people. He found himself scanning faces, posture, tone, and small changes in expression for signs that someone might harm him. If a door shut hard in the office or a phone rang sharply beside him, he would jolt in his chair, his body reacting before he could tell himself where he was. Coverage involving families or scenes with distressed children was particularly difficult. The sound of kids crying in field recordings or video clips could make his chest tighten and his attention narrow abruptly. On days when he felt dizzy or lightheaded for any reason, even from fatigue, it frightened him because the sensation felt too close to what he had experienced during the torture.

Over time he pulled away from people he had once seen easily. He stopped meeting former friends and colleagues socially, especially those who had known him before the detention. It felt intolerable to be with people who might compare who he had been with who he was now, or who might look too long and somehow recognize what he believed was wrong with him. His life grew narrower after work. He often stayed home alone, telling himself it was easier than being seen.

He also began restricting food. He described under-eating as a way of coping, something he turned to rather than a loss of appetite he could not explain. Alongside this, he spent long stretches dwelling on how the event could have been prevented. He replayed choices, names, timings, and conversations, searching for the moment when a different decision might have changed everything. The thinking did not lead to resolution, but he returned to it repeatedly, as if he should be able to account for the disaster if he looked hard enough.

By the time he sought help, the accumulation had become difficult to hide. His work had become more strained; he was still functioning, but ordinary newsroom sounds, recorded audio, and the constant need to read other people left him tense and depleted. Socially he was increasingly isolated. What finally brought him in was not one dramatic collapse but the recognition that his world had shrunk to managing reactions and avoiding exposure. He said he wanted help because he could no longer tell whether he was protecting himself or disappearing. What frightened him most was that the torture had revealed something fundamentally defective in him, and what he hoped, cautiously, was that he might find a way to live with the fragments of what happened without feeling that everyone could see it written on him.
